body:
Why technology matters in disaster management

Disaster management involves reducing risks before a hazardous event, protecting people and essential services during an emergency, and supporting recovery afterwards. Technology improves these activities by helping authorities observe hazards, understand which places and people may be affected, communicate warnings and assess damage.

However, technology is a means of supporting disaster management, not a substitute for preparedness or responsible decision-making. A satellite may identify floodwater, but the information protects people only when it is interpreted correctly, communicated to the appropriate authorities and converted into timely action.

Understanding the relationship between hazard information and disaster risk

A hazard is a potentially damaging event or process, such as a flood, cyclone, earthquake, landslide or industrial chemical release. Exposure refers to people, buildings, infrastructure and other assets located where they may be affected. Vulnerability describes conditions that make exposed people or assets more likely to suffer harm. Capacity includes the resources, knowledge, institutions and skills available to reduce that harm.

For example, knowing that a river may overflow is hazard information. Identifying nearby settlements, schools, hospitals, low-lying roads and people who may need assistance makes the information useful for risk assessment. Preparing safe routes, communicating warnings and conducting evacuation drills strengthen capacity.

A hazard map does not automatically show the likely number of casualties. Disaster risk also depends on exposure, vulnerability and capacity.

The information-to-action process

Effective disaster management connects several activities rather than treating each technology as a separate solution.

  1. Observe: Obtain information from satellites, weather instruments, river gauges, drones and reports from people in the affected area.
  2. Verify and analyse: Check the reliability, location and time of the information. Compare it with maps of settlements, roads, important facilities and known vulnerabilities.
  3. Decide: Responsible authorities assess the situation and identify suitable actions, such as issuing warnings, preparing shelters or arranging assistance.
  4. Communicate and act: Deliver understandable information through reliable channels and carry out the applicable disaster management plan.
  5. Review: Compare the expected and actual results and use the findings to improve future plans, data and training.

Applications across the disaster management cycle

StageUse of technologyUse of preparedness
Before a disasterHazard mapping, risk assessment, monitoring and forecastingTraining, public awareness, safety plans and mock drills
During a disasterWarnings, communications, situation maps and damage observationsCoordinated response, shelter arrangements and public precautions
After a disasterDamage assessment, updated maps and recovery monitoringRestoring services, reviewing actions and improving future readiness

These stages are connected. For example, satellite-based flood maps prepared during previous monsoons can help identify areas requiring special attention before the next monsoon. Observations collected during the next flood may then improve those maps.

The central role of institutions and people

Scientific agencies provide observations and forecasts; disaster management authorities coordinate planning and decisions; local institutions and communities carry out protective actions. Volunteers, teachers, hospital workers, industry personnel and residents need to understand what warnings mean and what their responsibilities are.

A warning that arrives in time but cannot be understood or acted upon is insufficient. Similarly, a detailed disaster management plan has limited practical value if the people responsible for implementing it have never been trained.

Prelims focus

  • Remote sensing, GIS and field observations help authorities understand hazards and exposure.
  • Risk assessment considers hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity.
  • Preparedness includes plans, training, public awareness and exercises.
  • Technology supports prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery.
  • Trap: Detecting a hazard is not the same as delivering an effective warning or ensuring public safety.

[Sources: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), Disaster Risk Reduction Terminology, entries on Early Warning System and Preparedness; National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Disaster Management Support, Overview; consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Technology and Preparedness: How Disaster Information Becomes Protective Action

body:
Meaning of remote sensing

Remote sensing is the acquisition of information about an object, area or phenomenon by a sensor that is not in direct physical contact with it.

A satellite observing floodwater is an example of remote sensing. The satellite carries instruments called sensors, which record electromagnetic energy associated with features on the Earth's surface. Aircraft and drones can also carry remote-sensing sensors.

The information collected by a sensor is processed into images or other data products. Analysts then interpret these products to identify features, detect changes and prepare maps.

Passive and active remote sensing

The important distinction is the source of the energy used for observation.

TypeHow it worksDisaster-related use or limitation
Passive optical sensingRecords sunlight reflected by the Earth's surfaceUseful for observing land cover and visible flood conditions; clouds and darkness limit observation
Passive thermal sensingRecords thermal radiation emitted by objectsHelps detect temperature differences and some active fires
Active radar sensingTransmits microwave signals and measures the returned signalMany radar systems can observe the surface through cloud cover and in darkness

Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is an active radar imaging technique. Its ability to operate in darkness and through many cloud conditions makes it especially useful during monsoon floods, when ordinary optical images may be obscured.

Radar is not completely free from limitations. Terrain, viewing conditions, vegetation and characteristics of the surface can complicate interpretation. A satellite image also cannot automatically establish whether a damaged building is structurally safe.

Four important types of resolution

The usefulness of satellite data depends partly on the characteristics of the sensor.

  • Spatial resolution: The level of ground detail distinguishable in an image. A smaller ground pixel generally allows finer features to be identified.
  • Temporal resolution: How frequently the same area can be observed. Frequent observations are particularly valuable when flood conditions or other hazards change rapidly.
  • Spectral resolution: The ability to record information in different wavelength bands. Different bands help distinguish water, vegetation, soil and other surfaces.
  • Radiometric resolution: The ability to distinguish small differences in recorded radiation intensity.

Spatial resolution concerns detail; temporal resolution concerns observation frequency. A very detailed image obtained several days earlier may be less useful for a rapidly changing emergency than a more recent image.

Major applications in disaster management

Floods and cyclones

Satellite images can identify the extent of inundation and help compare current flooding with earlier observations. Combining flood maps with settlements, roads and agricultural areas supports estimates of affected locations and planning for relief.

Cyclone-related satellite observations help monitor weather systems. Disaster management maps can also display forecast tracks supplied by the responsible meteorological agency. A satellite-derived map of flooded land and an official forecast of future flooding are different information products.

Drought and forest fires

Repeated observations of vegetation, soil moisture indicators and land conditions help assess agricultural drought. Such assessments should be considered alongside rainfall and other information because vegetation stress can have more than one cause.

Thermal observations can help detect active fires. Satellite-based detection supports awareness of possible fire locations, but cloud cover, spatial resolution and the timing of satellite observations can affect what is detected.

Landslides, earthquakes and damage assessment

Satellite imagery supports landslide inventories, terrain mapping and comparisons of areas before and after an event. After an earthquake, high-resolution images can help identify visibly damaged areas and disrupted infrastructure.

Change detection compares observations from different dates. For example, an image obtained before a major flood and another obtained afterwards may reveal newly inundated areas. The analyst must still check whether differences are caused by the disaster, seasonal changes or differences in image quality.

Indian applications

The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), under ISRO, provides satellite-based disaster management support. Its activities include flood and cyclone monitoring, flood hazard mapping, forest-fire information, drought studies and landslide-related mapping.

The distinction between two major satellite applications is important. Earth-observation satellites acquire information about the Earth's surface, while communication satellites support the transmission of information. Some satellite systems also support meteorological observation. The Indian Remote Sensing satellite series and the INSAT system are associated with these different functions.

Prelims focus

  • Remote sensing obtains information without direct physical contact with the observed object.
  • Passive sensors record naturally available radiation; active radar supplies its own signal.
  • SAR is particularly useful for flood mapping during extensive cloud cover.
  • Spatial, temporal, spectral and radiometric resolution describe different sensor capabilities.
  • NRSC is an ISRO centre that provides disaster management support.
  • Trap: A satellite observation is not automatically a validated damage estimate or an official public warning.

[Sources: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, Introduction to Remote Sensing, printed pp. 84–99; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 10, Transport and Communication, printed pp. 122–123; NRSC, Disaster Management Support, Applications and Sensors sections; consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Remote Sensing: Satellite Observation, Sensors and Disaster Applications

body:
What is a Geographic Information System?

A Geographic Information System (GIS) is a system for capturing, storing, managing, analysing and displaying information connected to geographic locations.

GIS is more than an electronic map. It can combine information from different sources and examine the relationships between places, hazards, people and infrastructure.

For example, a district authority may have a satellite-derived flood map, a map of villages, population information, a road network and the locations of hospitals. GIS allows these datasets to be examined together.

How GIS layers support disaster planning

A GIS layer contains information about a particular category of features. Common disaster management layers include:

  • Hazards: Flood-prone areas, landslide zones, previous inundation and observed disaster locations.
  • Exposure: Settlements, population, schools, hospitals, roads, power facilities and other assets.
  • Vulnerability: Information about people or places that may require additional assistance, where such information is available and appropriately protected.
  • Capacity: Shelters, available facilities, communication resources and planned routes.

A flood-planning example

Suppose a new satellite image shows water covering part of a district. A GIS analyst places the observed flood layer over maps of villages, roads, schools and health facilities. This identifies which mapped assets appear to lie within the observed inundation area.

The authority can then consider which roads are likely to be inaccessible, which settlements need verification and which facilities may be suitable for assistance. However, a road shown outside the inundation layer is not necessarily safe: bridges, fallen trees, landslides and rapidly changing water levels may still affect access.

Overlay analysis means examining multiple geographic layers together. Its output is useful for decisions, but the underlying information must be accurate and sufficiently recent.

GIS, GPS and remote sensing are different

TechnologyMain functionDisaster application
Remote sensingObserves features without direct physical contactIdentifies floodwater or visible damage
GPS or other satellite navigation systemsDetermines position and supports navigationRecords the location of an incident or facility
GISCombines, analyses and displays location-based informationRelates hazards to exposed people, roads and services

A field worker may use GPS to record the coordinates of a damaged bridge. Remote sensing may provide imagery of the surrounding area. GIS can bring both sources together with the road network and settlement data.

Decision Support Systems

A Decision Support System (DSS) combines relevant information and analytical tools to help people compare conditions and possible actions. In disaster management, it may display current hazards, affected areas, facilities and available resources.

Decision support does not remove the responsibility of authorised officials to evaluate the evidence and make decisions. A DSS can show that a settlement lies in an exposed area, but local authorities must consider current field conditions, the needs of residents and available resources before acting.

Indian geospatial disaster systems

The National Database for Emergency Management (NDEM), developed through NRSC, is a national repository of GIS-based information with decision-support tools for disaster and emergency management. NRSC also provides disaster-related information through Bhuvan, ISRO's geospatial platform.

These resources help users visualise flood extent, historical hazard information and other geographic data. Their purpose is to improve situational awareness and support planning. They should not be confused with the authorities responsible for issuing official public warnings.

Prelims focus

  • GIS integrates and analyses geographic information from multiple layers.
  • Overlay analysis can connect a hazard map with settlements, roads and important facilities.
  • GPS provides position information; GIS performs broader spatial analysis.
  • NDEM provides GIS-based information and decision-support tools through NRSC.
  • Bhuvan is an ISRO geospatial platform.
  • Trap: A mapped route or shelter may become unsuitable when actual conditions change.

[Sources: NRSC, Disaster Management Support, Overview and National Database for Emergency Management sections; NRSC, Bhuvan Disaster Management Support, Flood and Cyclone Monitoring; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, information extraction and thematic maps, printed pp. 90 and 98–99; consulted 2 November 2026.]
